name: TCP vs UDP
intent: Choose between a transport that guarantees every byte arrives in order (TCP) and one that just sends packets as fast as it can and accepts losses (UDP), based on whether late data is still useful.
scenario: A file download and a live video call run over the same lossy Wi-Fi. For the download, every byte matters and a delay is fine. For the call, a frame that arrives half a second late is worse than a frame that never arrives.
problem: Networks drop, delay and reorder packets. Applications have different needs: some need perfect, ordered data, others need low delay above all. A single transport cannot be best for both, so the internet offers two with opposite trade-offs, and picking the wrong one makes a download corrupt or a call stutter.

howItWorks.title: TCP builds a reliable ordered stream
howItWorks.text: TCP first sets up a connection with a handshake. It numbers every byte, the receiver acknowledges what it has, and the sender retransmits anything not acknowledged in time. Data is handed to the application in order, so the application sees a clean stream even when the network is messy.

howItWorks.title: TCP also protects the network
howItWorks.text: It slows down when it detects loss or congestion (congestion control) and uses flow control so a fast sender does not overwhelm a slow receiver. This keeps shared links usable, at the cost of throttling the sender when the network is busy.

howItWorks.title: The price is delay when packets are lost
howItWorks.text: If packet 5 is lost, packets 6, 7 and 8 may already have arrived, but TCP cannot give them to the application until 5 is retransmitted and received. Everything behind the gap waits (head-of-line blocking). On a clean network this never shows; on a lossy one it shows as stalls.

howItWorks.title: UDP sends independent datagrams
howItWorks.text: UDP has no connection, no acknowledgements and no retransmission. Each datagram is sent on its own and may arrive, arrive out of order, or vanish. It is fast and has minimal overhead, and the application decides what to do about loss.

howItWorks.title: Build only what you need on top of UDP
howItWorks.text: Real-time media drops late packets and conceals the gap. Games send the latest position and ignore old ones. DNS sends one small request and retries itself. QUIC, the transport under HTTP/3, builds reliability and congestion control on UDP in a way that avoids TCP's head-of-line blocking between streams.

pros: TCP: every byte arrives, in order, with congestion control built in
UDP: lowest delay, no handshake, no blocking behind lost packets
UDP lets the application choose what reliability it needs
cons: TCP: handshake delay, and stalls behind a lost packet
TCP: one slow, lossy path slows the whole stream
UDP: no delivery guarantee, no ordering, and no congestion control unless you build it
UDP is often blocked or rate limited by firewalls, and easy to abuse for amplification attacks
whenToUse: TCP for web pages, APIs, file transfer, email and databases: correctness first
UDP for live voice and video, games, DNS queries, telemetry and discovery
UDP-based protocols such as QUIC when you want reliability without head-of-line blocking
whenNotToUse: UDP for data that must not be lost, unless you add your own acknowledgements and retransmission
TCP for real-time media where late data is worthless
pitfalls: Writing your own reliability on top of UDP and getting congestion control wrong, which harms the network
Sending large UDP datagrams that get fragmented and lost
Assuming TCP is always slower: for bulk transfers it usually is the right tool
Ignoring that TCP connection setup adds a round trip before any data
